title: Black mirrors: ...b6 and ...Bd6
intro:
Black plays ...b6 and ...Bb7 and builds the same structure you are building, one move behind. It is the most sensible answer to the Zukertort and the one that asks the hardest question: if both bishops point down the long diagonal, whose is doing more?

## Whose diagonal is it

Yours, for one reason: you are a move ahead, and the square in the middle of both diagonals is e5, not e4. Your knight can stand on e5 supported by the d4 pawn. Black's knight cannot stand on e4 supported by a d5 pawn, because a pawn on d5 does not defend e4. That single asymmetry is the whole difference between the two setups.

## What that means over the board

Get to Ne5 first. Once the knight is there with the bishop on b2 behind it, the mirror stops being a mirror: Black has a bishop staring at a square White already owns.

## The bishop on d6

Black often adds ...Bd6, which is the honest attempt to fight for e5. Then the fork from chapter 1 is back on: if Black ever takes on e5, the recapture with the d-pawn attacks the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6 at once. Watch for it every time, because a mirror position makes trades look automatic and this one is not.

## The bishop to a6

Some players go ...Ba6 instead, offering to trade off White's attacking bishop. Take it: the trade costs Black time, the knight is left on a6 where it does nothing, and the b2 bishop and the knight on e5 were always the pieces that mattered here.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Letting Black play ...Ne4 and ...f5 unchallenged, which turns the mirror into a Stonewall and gives Black the square you wanted. Trading on b7 for no reason and helping Black's knight to a good square. Playing Ne5 without the bishop on b2 behind it. And missing the fork on d6 and f6 because both sides look the same.
